steps.user_message: I'm preparing my 2024 taxes and could use your help. Situation: married filing jointly, Seattle WA. W-2 from Acme Corp: $88,100. Side income: $14,600 from web design (2 clients). Interest $1,780 (Chase savings), dividends $440 (Robinhood). Home office: 155 sq ft, rent $1,600/month, apartment 680 sq ft. Deductions: student loan interest $4,400 (EdFinancial, 2017–2020); charity $1,100 to Local United Way with receipt; unreimbursed expenses $720. Can you help me figure out deductions, standard vs itemized, and home office treatment—and which forms to use?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — this is enough to give a clear, practical plan. I ran the numbers roughly and listed exactly which forms you’ll use and what I need from you to finish the calculations. A few clarifying questions are at the end.

Quick summary / likely outcome
- You will almost certainly use the standard deduction (married filing jointly) — your itemizable amounts (only $1,100 charitable) are far below the standard deduction, so itemizing likely won’t help.
- Your side (self‑employment) activity must be reported on Schedule C and will be subject to self‑employment tax (Schedule SE). You can take a home‑office deduction (if the space is used exclusively and regularly for the business). The regular method (allocating rent) will produce a much larger home‑office deduction than the simplified method for your numbers, but it requires Form 8829 and may be limited by your Schedule C net profit rules.
- You should expect to file: Form 1040 (with Schedule 1), Schedule C, Schedule SE, Schedule B (because interest > $1,500), and possibly Form 8829 (regular home office) or Form 8995 (QBI deduction) if applicable. If you itemize (unlikely) file Schedule A.

Key numeric estimates (rounding to nearest dollar)
Inputs you gave:
- W‑2 (Acme): $88,100
- Self‑employment (web design): $14,600
- Interest (Chase): $1,780
- Dividends (Robinhood): $440 (qualified)
- Rent: $1,600/mo = $19,200/yr; home office 155 sq ft of 680 sq ft = 155/680 ≈ 22.79%
- Student loan interest reported: $4,400 (see clarifying Qs)
- Charitable: $1,100
- Business “unreimbursed expenses”: $720 (need to confirm these are business expenses)

Home‑office comparison (two common methods)
1) Simplified method: $5/sq ft × 155 sq ft = $775 home‑office deduction.
- Estimated Schedule C net profit = 14,600 − 720 (business expenses) − 775 = $13,105
- Approx SE tax: 13,105 × 92.35% × 15.3% ≈ $1,852
- Half of SE tax (deductible adjustment to income) ≈ $926

2) Regular method (rent allocation only used here as example):
- Rent allocable to business = $19,200 × (155/680) ≈ $4,374
- Estimated Schedule C net profit = 14,600 − 720 − 4,374 = $9,506
- Approx SE tax: 9,506 × 92.35% × 15.3% ≈ $1,343
- Half of SE tax ≈ $672

Takeaway from comparison:
- Regular method (if you can/want to allocate rent and other home expenses) gives a much larger deduction than the simplified method for your numbers and lowers both income tax and SE tax. But it requires Form 8829, supporting documentation of shared expenses, and must meet exclusive/regular-use rules. Also, home office regular‑method deductions cannot exceed your net business income; any excess is carried forward per Form 8829 rules.
- If you prefer simplicity and minimal recordkeeping, use the simplified method ($775). If you want the larger deduction and you can document shared expenses, use the regular method.

Other important items
- Student loan interest: the maximum deduction is $2,500 (subject to MAGI phase‑outs). The $4,400 you listed exceeds the deduction cap — you can only deduct up to the allowed amount actually paid in the tax year (and phaseouts apply). Confirm how much interest was actually paid in 2024 and whether you received Form 1098‑E for 2024.
- Schedule B is required because your taxable interest ($1,780) is > $1,500.
- Qualified dividends are reported on Form 1040 and may be taxed at preferential rates; with your income level they’re small but should be entered correctly. You generally won’t need Schedule D unless you have capital gains/losses to report beyond the dividend entries.
- You may be eligible for the QBI (Section 199A) deduction — up to 20% of qualified business income in many cases. With your likely taxable income, you’re probably under the phaseout thresholds and able to claim the simplified QBI computation (Form 8995). It’s worth checking because it could reduce taxable income by up to roughly 20% of your qualified business income.
- State return: Washington State has no state income tax, so no state return for wages. (But if you have local/property taxes or other obligations that matter, mention them.)
- Estimated tax: because you have self‑employment income, you may need to make or have made estimated tax payments (Form 1040‑ES) to cover income and SE taxes not covered by W‑2 withholding.

Which forms you will likely need
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1 (Additional Income and Adjustments) — business income flows through here (from Schedule C adjustments)
- Schedule C — profit/loss from your web‑design business
- Schedule SE — self‑employment tax
- Schedule B — interest and ordinary dividends (required because interest > $1,500)
- Form 8829 — Expenses for Business Use of Your Home (if you choose the regular home‑office method)
- Schedule A — only if you itemize (unlikely here)
- Form 8995 (or 8995‑A) — Qualified Business Income deduction (if applicable)
- Form 1099‑NEC or 1099‑MISC — if your clients issued these to you (you still report the income whether or not you have 1099s)
- Form 1040‑ES — if you need to make estimated tax payments

Action items / questions for you (needed to finalize numbers)
1. Are the $720 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses for the web‑design work (software, hosting, supplies, etc.)? If they were unreimbursed employee expenses for an employer job, they are not deductible on your federal return.
2. How much student loan interest was actually paid in 2024? Do you have Form 1098‑E (EdFinancial) for 2024? (You listed $4,400 — confirm whether that is 2024 interest paid.)
3. Do you have any other business expenses (computer equipment, software subscriptions, hosting fees, advertising, mileage, contractor payments) or 1099s from clients?
4. Do you use the 155‑sq‑ft space exclusively and regularly for business (required for the deduction)? Do you pay any separate utilities, renter’s insurance, or internet that you want to allocate to the business?
5. Do you want the simpler approach (simplified home‑office method) or do you plan to document rent/utilities and use the regular method (Form 8829)?
6. Have you made any estimated tax payments in 2024, or do you prefer to increase W‑2 withholding to cover the SE tax?

Next steps I can take for you
- If you want, I can compute a more precise draft tax worksheet (estimated AGI, tax, SE tax, and estimated refund/amount due) once you confirm answers to the questions above and provide:
  - confirmation of the $720 as business expenses (and a short itemized list)
  - exact student‑loan interest paid in 2024 (and whether 1098‑E is available)
  - any other business costs and whether you want to use regular or simplified home‑office method
  - any 1099s you received
- I can also draft a checklist of receipts and documentation you should keep for Form 8829 and Schedule C.

If you want, tell me:
- (A) confirm whether the $720 is business expense and list other business expenses, and
- (B) confirm student loan interest paid in 2024 (or whether you want me to assume the full $4,400 was paid).

I’ll run the detailed worksheet and produce a suggested filing breakdown and estimated tax due/refund after you confirm.
